prompt.context: The client is the CEO of a power company that does the following things related to power: generation, distribution, links regions with grids, buys energy wholesale and re-sells it, retails energy by selling it directly to consumers. The company generates several types of energy: coal, natural gas, wind, nuclear, and solar. This case focuses on coal power generation. Lately, the client has experienced a profitability decline (about $100MM less than target) in its core business of generating power and has hired McKinsey to diagnose the problem.
prompt.question: The client's coal power generation business is $100MM below profit target. Diagnose the profitability problem and recommend a path forward.

clarifying_info.q: How many power plants does the client operate?
clarifying_info.a: 10 power plants, each with capacity of 4.5MM megawatt hours per year, currently running at 80% of capacity.

clarifying_info.q: What is the revenue per megawatt hour?
clarifying_info.a: They sell each megawatt hour for $40.
Coal-related (variable) costs are $10 per megawatt hour. Fixed costs allocated across current capacity are $5 per megawatt hour.

framework: Profitability = Revenue – Costs; diagnose which side is driving the $100MM shortfall
Revenue driver: volume (capacity utilization) × price per MWh
Cost drivers: variable coal costs per MWh, fixed cost allocation
Identify whether the gap is revenue-side (low utilization or low price) or cost-side (higher input costs, higher fixed costs)
If utilization is the lever, quantify the profit impact of increasing it and then investigate root causes of underutilization

questions.prompt: Calculate current annual profit at 80% capacity utilization.
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a clean P&L: Revenue = plants × capacity × utilization × price; Variable cost = plants × capacity × utilization × variable cost/MWh; Fixed cost = total MWh produced × fixed cost/MWh; Profit = Revenue – Variable cost – Fixed cost.

math.setup: 10 plants × 4.5MM MWh/plant/year = 45MM MWh total capacity. At 80% utilization: 36MM MWh produced.

questions.prompt: If the client increased capacity utilization to 90%, what would be the impact on profit?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that fixed costs do not change with utilization (already allocated across current capacity), so incremental profit = incremental MWh × (price – variable cost). Alternatively, candidate can recompute the full P&L at 90% and compare. Strong candidates note the $135MM increase exceeds the $100MM shortfall, restoring profitability.

math.setup: At 90% utilization: 10 × 4.5MM × 90% = 40.5MM MWh produced. Incremental MWh vs 80% = 40.5MM – 36MM = 4.5MM MWh.
steps: Shortcut: 4.5MM incremental MWh × ($40 – $10) = $135MM (fixed cost per MWh also changes, reconcile with full P&L)
Note: using the casebook's stated result, the increase is $135MM
math.answer: Profit increases by approximately $135MM, bringing profit above the $100MM shortfall target

questions.prompt: Brainstorm reasons why the plants have only been operating at 80% capacity.
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure reasons into buckets such as demand-side, supply-side, and internal/company issues. See brainstorming section.

brainstorming.prompt: The client wants to pursue the strategy of increasing utilization. Brainstorm reasons why the plants have only been operating at 80% capacity to date.

categories.name: Demand
ideas: Insufficient demand in the regions served
Customers switching to alternative energy sources
Pricing too high relative to competing suppliers

categories.name: Supply / Input constraints
ideas: Coal supply shortages or procurement issues
Environmental or regulatory constraints limiting output

categories.name: Internal / Company issues
ideas: Operational bottlenecks in the generation process

recommendation: Under-utilized capacity is a key driver of the $100MM profitability shortfall
Increasing capacity utilization from 80% to 90% would add approximately $135MM in profit, more than closing the gap
risks: Root cause of underutilization is unknown; raising utilization may not be feasible without addressing underlying constraints
If demand is the constraint, pushing utilization could lead to unsold power and wasted costs
next_steps: Investigate and diagnose the specific reasons why plants are operating at only 80% capacity (demand, supply, or internal issues)
Prioritize the most actionable lever based on root cause
Develop an implementation plan to close the utilization gap
